tldr: This research predicts contact locations and interaction forces with high accuracy from human egocentric (first-person RGB) video, transferring and utilizing them as tactile inputs for robot hands through anatomical region correspondences.
hero_caption: An overall framework that adapts a visual-tactile prediction model learned from human data to robot hands via anatomical correspondences. The adapted model functions as a 'virtual tactile sensor,' providing tactile signals for both simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot imitation learning (VLA).
overview:
When robots perform contact-rich tasks like removing a pen cap or turning a bottle cap, knowing where and how much force is being applied is essential. However, estimating contact forces from vision alone is difficult because fingertips and objects get occluded. Meanwhile, physical tactile sensors for robots are expensive and fragile, and their layouts vary from hand to hand, making large-scale tactile data collection extremely challenging.

To address this, the authors focused on the fact that human egocentric video can be collected at scale. They proposed 'Ego2Contact,' a framework that learns a visual-tactile prior from videos of humans wearing tactile gloves and transfers it to robot hands. Although human and robot hands differ drastically in appearance and sensor layouts, they successfully bridged this morphological gap by defining hand anatomical regions (fingertips, intermediate joints, palms, etc.) as a shared interface.

In experiments, Ego2Contact not only outperformed prior methods in tactile prediction on unseen objects manipulated by humans, but also successfully adapted to both simulated and real-world robot hands. In simulated contact-rich tasks, policies using predicted touch significantly outperformed vision-only baselines and approached the performance of using ground-truth physical tactile sensors. It is an impressive study that opens up a way to skillfully control robots by letting them 'imagine' touch from video, even without physical sensors.
contributions: Proposed a Conditional Flow-Matching model that fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to generate continuous bimanual pressure fields with high accuracy.
Constructed a general-purpose interface linking human hands and differing robot sensor layouts across 17 anatomical regions, enabling bidirectional mapping.

Decoupled the tactile predictor completely from the control policy, demonstrating that it can supply tactile inputs to both simulated reinforcement learning (RL) and real-robot vision-language-action models (VLA).

sections.heading: We Want Tactile Sensing on Robots, but Hardware Barriers Are Too High
sections.summary: Tactile sensing is essential for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, but gathering robot tactile data is severely bottlenecked by hardware constraints. This paper presents 'Ego2Contact,' which learns tactile priors from easily collected human egocentric video and transfers them to robots via anatomical correspondences.
sections.details:
To achieve dexterous manipulation, robots need tactile feedback—such as tightening grip force right before slipping or sensing the exact moment of contact under visual occlusion. In practice, however, robotic tactile skins and optical tactile sensors break easily, and their designs differ across robot hand models. This makes creating a shared, large-scale tactile dataset across multiple robots nearly impossible.

Can we leverage human egocentric video instead? Using recordings of humans performing tasks with tactile gloves, we can train models that predict touch from video. However, previous studies remained confined to the domain of human hands and did not venture into controlling robots. Robot hands are made of metal and plastic, looking completely different from human hands, and their sensor counts and placements are entirely distinct.

Crucially, Ego2Contact solves this gap in appearance and sensor layout simultaneously. It builds an accurate tactile predictor combining temporal information with local hand appearance. By dividing the hand into 17 anatomical regions, it enables tactile information exchange with any robot hand morphology. Because the predictor runs as an independent module, another major advantage is that it is agnostic to the control policy architecture.

sections.heading: How Far Have Vision-Based Touch Estimation and Robot Transfer Come?
sections.summary: Prior works have predicted touch from video or had robots imagine touch, but there was no unified mechanism to directly transfer tactile priors learned from large-scale human data to diverse robot control policies.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into three categories:

### Vision-based Contact and Pressure Estimation
Estimating contact from images began with binary estimation of 'where contact occurs.' Recently, combined with tactile glove data, it has evolved into estimating continuous pressure across the entire hand. A notable example is TouchAnything, which treats each hand as a canonical $21\times 21$ grid. However, these methods evaluated their predictions solely on human hands.

### Tactile Sensing and Imagination for Robot Manipulation
To bypass the difficulty of deploying physical tactile sensors permanently on robots, methods like TacImag predict touch from vision using the robot's own demonstrations, while ViTacWorld learns a visual-tactile world model. Yet, these rely exclusively on data collected on a specific robot platform, failing to leverage the vast and diverse interaction data available from humans.

### Transferring Human Priors to Robot Tactile Learning
Studies such as VTDexManip and H-Tac have brought tactile knowledge from human video to robots. However, their tactile estimation is tightly coupled with a specific reinforcement learning architecture or action space, making it difficult to plug into different robots or policies. Ego2Contact stands apart by isolating the perception module and outputting tactile observations through anatomical correspondences.

sections.heading: Fusing Temporal Context and Cross-Body Adaptation via Anatomical Grids
sections.summary: Temporal context and hand-local features are extracted from consecutive input RGB frames to generate bimanual tactile maps using Conditional Flow-Matching. A bidirectional mapping across 17 hand regions enables both fine-tuning with robot sensor values and conversion into policy inputs.
sections.details:
### Problem Formulation
The model takes an RGB video clip $V_t$ of the past $T=8$ frames sampled at stride $\Delta=2$. From this, it predicts a $21\times 21$ tactile pressure field $P_t \in [0, 1]^{2\times 21\times 21}$ for both hands. Each hand has 217 active sensor cells.

### Learning the Visual-Tactile Prior
Because contact surfaces are frequently occluded by the hand, static appearance or 3D poses alone cannot accurately estimate pressure. Therefore, the model is supplied with both temporal context and local hand appearance:
- Scene temporal context: A frozen DINOv2 (ViT-B/14) extracts 256 tokens per frame, which are aggregated across time using a 3-layer Temporal Transformer.
- Hand-local cues: Features are extracted from hand crops using a frozen WiLoR (ViT-H) and spatially pooled down to 16 tokens per hand.
- Feature fusion: Hand tokens serve as queries in Cross-Attention over the temporal scene tokens to produce conditioning vector $c_t$.

For the tactile generator, a 6-block Diffusion Transformer (DiT) with Rectified Flow (which predicts flow velocity to generate images from noise) generates the $21\times 21$ grid. The loss function incorporates a contact-weighted loss that places higher penalties on contacting cells, alongside total variation (TV) regularization to smooth abrupt jumps between neighboring cells.

### Robot Adaptation via Anatomical Correspondences
This is the most intriguing mechanism. The 217 output cells are grouped into 17 anatomical regions, such as individual finger joints and the palm.
- Forward mapping (Training): Robot measurements are mapped into the canonical $21\times 21$ grid. Contact forces on rigid simulator links are spread across regional cells using Gaussian weights, while readings from an 880-taxel real glove are averaged per cell. This standardizes data from either robot into uniform supervisory signals, allowing direct fine-tuning of the human-pretrained model.
- Inverse mapping (Policy execution): The predicted grid is converted into formats suited for robot policies. For reinforcement learning (PPO), it is compressed into a 34-dimensional vector containing the maximum regional pressure (17 continuous values) and contact indicators (17 binary flags). For real-world VLA ($N_0$-VTLA), a Ridge regression decoder reconstructs the 880 taxels, which are rendered into a $224\times 224$ tactile image as policy input.

sections.heading: From Unseen Objects to Dexterous Manipulation: Does Predicted Touch Actually Help?
sections.summary: Ego2Contact outperformed prior methods on human tactile datasets, showing strong generalization especially on unseen objects. In simulated robot RL, it significantly outperformed non-tactile baselines, and it also successfully trained a VLA policy on a real robot.
sections.details:
### Tactile Prediction Accuracy on Human Data
Evaluated on the human dataset 'EgoTouch,' Ego2Contact outperformed TouchAnything, setting new state-of-the-art results in contact IoU (overlap of contact area), temporal agreement, and pressure MAE (mean absolute error). It demonstrated similarly superior performance when adapted to another benchmark, 'EgoTactile.'

To understand what drove this success, the authors conducted an ablation where local hand visual features were replaced with 3D hand poses. While this variant improved accuracy on objects seen during training, its contact IoU dropped drastically on unseen objects. Hand poses overfit to specific shapes in the training set; local visual cues like hand texture and object deformation proved vital for generalizing to unseen objects.

### Robot Adaptation and Simulation Control
After fine-tuning on roughly 70k frames from Isaac Gym, the grid contact IoU on robot data jumped dramatically from 0.008 (unadapted) to 0.476. Compared to adapted TouchAnything, Ego2Contact exhibited lower Center of Pressure error, pinpointing contact locations more accurately in space.

Providing this predicted touch online to PPO reinforcement learning policies yielded remarkable results:
- Bottle Cap Turning: Compared to the non-tactile baseline, the policy with predicted touch achieved a 71.0% success rate, coming remarkably close to the policy using ground-truth sensors (74.1%).
- In Lever Sliding and Bimanual Handover, it also significantly outperformed the non-tactile baseline.
- However, on Pen Cap Removal, where physical sensors achieved a 95.0% success rate, predicted touch reached only 1.0% (baseline was 0.0%). This highlights that tasks requiring millimeter-level interlocking of fingertips remain challenging when relying solely on video-predicted touch.

### Real-Robot Deployment
In the real-world setup, an xArm6 arm was equipped with a BrainCo Revo 2 hand wearing an 880-taxel tactile glove. The model was adapted using roughly 123k frames collected via VR teleoperation. Using the adapted model, tactile images were generated offline from past demonstration videos to post-train the VLA model '$N_0$-VTLA.' The policy operated stably at about 24.5 Hz across delicate real-world tasks such as test tube transfer and bottle decapping.

sections.heading: A New Way to Bring Touch from Humans to Robots 'Visually'
sections.summary: The authors established a framework to learn visual-tactile priors from human video and transfer them to robot hands via anatomical correspondences. They demonstrated that high-level manipulation is possible by generating virtual touch from vision, even in environments with restricted tactile hardware.
sections.details:
This study presented an approach to overcome severe robotic tactile data scarcity by tapping into human egocentric video, a highly scalable data source. Combining temporal context with local hand features in a Flow-Matching generator enabled precise touch prediction, and establishing a shared foundation of 17 anatomical regions demonstrated that tactile signals can be supplied to both simulation and real robots.

While predicted touch does not fully match ground-truth physical sensors across all tasks, its ability to compensate for touch through vision is deeply impactful—especially in harsh environments where sensors break or for low-cost robot hands that cannot carry tactile arrays.

As future work, the authors point to reducing the volume of paired data required for robot adaptation and constructing universal tactile representations that map automatically to any robot or sensor geometry without manual anatomical correspondence engineering.

takeaways: Scarcity of robot tactile data can be mitigated by transferring visual-tactile priors learned from human first-person tactile glove data.

Relying solely on 3D hand poses for contact estimation leads to overfitting on unseen objects; combining local visual features (e.g., WiLoR) capturing texture and deformation with temporal context is essential.
Using 17 anatomical regions based on hand skeleton structure as a shared interface allows unified handling of distinct robot sensor modalities, from rigid link forces to dense taxel arrays.
Predicted touch functions completely independently of policy architectures, serving directly as online RL state observations or offline tactile annotations for imitation learning (VLA).
limitations: Adapting to new robots still requires manual engineering effort to correspond robot links or taxels to the 17 anatomical regions.

For tasks demanding extremely precise alignment and stiff interlocking like pen cap removal, minor prediction errors from video are fatal, leaving a large performance gap compared to real physical sensors.
Fine-tuning to the robot domain still requires collecting a non-trivial amount (tens to hundreds of thousands of frames) of paired data.
